chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinanī, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who performed li'an (oath of imprecation) with his wife and disowned her child, then contradicted himself after the li'an, claiming the child was indeed his. I asked: Is his son returned to him? He said: 'No, and no honor; he is not returned to him, nor is she permissible to him until the Day of Judgment.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: His saying (peace be upon him) 'he is not returned to him' means that the child is not attached to him with a true attachment that causes the child to inherit him and he to inherit the child. Rather, his lineage is established on the condition that he inherits his father, but his father does not inherit him, according to what we have previously mentioned. And to add clarity to that is what we narrated:
ai.seo_question: What happens to inheritance and marital status if a man performs li'an but later claims the child is his?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records that if a husband repudiates his own claim after li'an, the child’s lineage is not fully re-established for mutual inheritance, meaning the father inherits from the child but the child does not inherit from the father. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential distinction between the permanence of the marital prohibition (haram) and the conditional nature of the lineage (nasab) following the oath of imprecation.
